Sequence length distribution and batching strategy
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez: hey everyone, thanks for joining, let's get started. we have 38 minutes, quick agenda — review last weeks numbers, kernel profiling, and next steps.
[00:20] Priya Desai: thanks, yeah we've been running the 8k sample workload, mostly 512 tokens median, a tail up to 2048 for some long docs, so that distribution is what we sent over.
[00:40] Liam Chen: got it, priya, that helps. quick recap: on our side we re-ran the TTFT benches on the dedicated A100 cluster and on hosted h100-optimized nodes, but note some of the labels in the logs are a bit off because the profiler swapped nv vs nvcc names.
[01:05] Marcus Lee: question — when you say TTFT are we measuring from request arrival to first token emission, or including network front door? we need to compare apples to apples.
[01:20] Sofia Martinez: good call — we're measuring server-side, request hit to first token emitted from the runtime; that excludes CDN and client jitter. i'll annotate the spreadsheet.
[01:35] Priya Desai: what numbers are we seeing?
[01:40] Liam Chen: baseline non-streaming TTFT on hosted h100-optimized was roughly 220ms median, p95 about 480ms, p99 around 820ms for 512-seq samples at concurrency 8. enabling streaming reduced median TTFT to ~120ms, p95 ~300ms, p99 ~620ms. these are rough because of queueing on the test harness.
[02:10] Priya Desai: ok 120ms seems good, our SLA target is p95 < 250ms for interactive flows, so streaming is promising.
[02:25] Hannah Rios: from security side we need to confirm audit logs and KMS usage for Dedicated — also latency for encryption shouldn't add more than 5-10ms ideally.
[02:40] Sofia Martinez: yes, we'll include KMS overhead numbers. for the dedicated pilot we can test with customer-managed KMS to measure impact.
[03:00] Marcus Lee: can you remind us about kernel choices? we saw flash-attn in the logs but sometimes it fell back to cutlass or triton kernels, which seemed slower.
[03:15] Liam Chen: right — flash-attn gives the best perf for attention on short to medium seq lengths, but on very long sequences or certain head sizes our runtime will choose a fallback (cutlass/triton) for numerical stability or memory layout. the profiler shows about 18-22% higher latency on fallback kernels.
[03:40] Priya Desai: is there a knob to force flash-attn so we can test? we tried forcing but ran into OOMs on the 2048 tails.
[03:55] Liam Chen: you can force it but risk OOM; better approach is to split by sequence-length routing: short sequences go to flash-attn instances, long sequences go to a long-seq pool where we accept the fallback. that reduces overall TTFT for interacive short queries.
[04:15] Sofia Martinez: that aligns with our smart routing plan — route by seq length and latency SLO.
[04:30] Priya Desai: ok, next metric — streaming chunk size. we tested chunk=16 vs chunk=64 and saw chunk=16 had better TTFT but slightly worse throughput overall.
[04:45] Liam Chen: yep smaller chunks lower first-byte latency but increase compute overhead; there's a sweet spot typically 8-32 depending on model. we saw 16 is good for your workload.
[05:05] Marcus Lee: batching window — we set to 25ms, but there were spikes to 50ms when concurrency jumped, any suggestions?
[05:20] Liam Chen: you can do adaptive batching with a cap on max latency. set a small fixed window for low concurrency and enable dynamic expansion during burst. also prefix/KV cache hit rate matters a lot — your workload is caching a lot of repeated prefixes which helped reduce token compute.
[05:40] Priya Desai: about quantization — we ran int8 in the pilot and saw slightly higher p99s for some ops, is that expected?
[05:50] Liam Chen: int8 quant gives big throughput and cost wins, but can change kernel selection and sometimes increases variance in tail. we recommend model-level QA and evals; for interactive low-latency set we often use float16 with kernel-level optimizations first, then test int8 on a long-run dedicated bench.
[06:10] Hannah Rios: for the security checklist, can you put the SOC2/ISO docs and the PCA redaction notes in the same folder? helps us map requirements to the pilot.
[06:25] Sofia Martinez: will do. link will be in the follow-up.
[06:35] Priya Desai: back to TTFT — do we have per-operation breakdown? e.g., tokenization, embedding lookup, attention, kv cache ops? that would help isolate the 300-600ms p95 steps.
[06:50] Liam Chen: yes the kernel profiler has breakdowns. quick glance: tokenization negligible (<5ms), embedding lookup depends if you use on-disk or in-memory, attention kernels dominated — on fallback kernels attention took ~35-45% of the TTFT delta. kv cache plumbing adds ~10-20ms when cold.
[07:15] Marcus Lee: cold vs warm cache — what's our observed warm hit ratio?
[07:25] Priya Desai: in our traces warm hit is about 78% for the interactive flows, but batch jobs drop that to 40% which explains some tail.
[07:40] Liam Chen: so immediate wins: increase prefix caching for session-based queries, and consider sticky routing for interactive sessions to keep KV-locality.
[07:55] Priya Desai: agreed. on the dedicated tests, what about hardware differences — we saw H100 does better on larger batches but slightly worse median TTFT for tiny sequences?
[08:10] Liam Chen: correct — H100 kernel fusion favors throughput at larger sequence lengths and batch sizes; A100 sometimes gives lower latency for tiny batches due to different warp/block scheduling. depends on your profile. we can run the same workload across both and dump comparative plots.
[08:30] Sofia Martinez: let's plan a cross-hardware comparison as an action item.
[08:40] Marcus Lee: can you share the raw benchmark spreadsheet again? the one with columns — ttft_med, p95, p99, chunk_size, seq_len, kernel_type, gpu_type, concurrency.
[08:55] Liam Chen: yes, will upload; note that some column names got munged during export (kernel_type sometimes shows truncated names). i'll clean that.
[09:10] Priya Desai: about acceptance criteria — we want p95 < 250ms and p99 < 600ms for interactive. is that feasible without major infra changes?
[09:25] Liam Chen: yes achievable with streaming + sequence-routing + kernel pinning for short seqs. we may need a small dedicated pool for interactive with flash-attn enabled and tuned batch windows. cost vs latency tradeoff we'll outline.
[09:40] Hannah Rios: on the compliance side, if we run Dedicated behind their VPC with customer KMS, does Redwood still provide audit logs? retention will be our responsibility but we need to confirm retention windows and export format.
[09:58] Sofia Martinez: yes, Dedicated supports audit log export to your S3 and we can stream to your SIEM; retention can be configured, we'll include supported retention durations in the doc.
[10:10] Priya Desai: any blockers on our side? we need to produce realistic session traces and seq distribution.
[10:20] Marcus Lee: we'll schedule a small batch to capture traces this week.
[10:28] Sofia Martinez: ok, short recap then next steps — liam will share kernel profile and cleaned spreadsheets, sofia will send pricing and links to security artifacts, priya and marcus will share seq distribution and session traces. we plan kernel tuning workshop next tuesday.
[10:45] Priya Desai: sounds good, thanks all.
[10:50] Hannah Rios: thanks, bye.
[10:55] Sofia Martinez: thanks everyone, meeting adjourned.
